lesson_title: The Fingerprint at the Second Layer
hook_text: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35 — the jumps keep growing. But dig one layer down and this pattern just left its fingerprint.
clip_script: Look at this sequence: three, eight, fifteen, twenty-four, thirty-five. The jumps are five, seven, nine, eleven — growing every time. Grade ten patterns never did that; their steps repeated. So is this chaos? Dig one layer down. Check the gaps BETWEEN the gaps: five to seven — two. Seven to nine — two. Nine to eleven — two. Steady. That steadiness is a fingerprint, and it identifies the culprit instantly: a QUADRATIC pattern, the family of n squared. And the fingerprint doesn't just name the family — it measures it. That steady number at the bottom is always DOUBLE the coefficient of n squared. Steady two? Built on one n squared. Steady six? Three n squared. Steady negative? The pattern climbs, turns, and comes back down like a ball in the air. From there, three quick facts assemble the whole formula: halve the bottom number for a, the first jump gives b, the first term gives c. T n equals n squared plus two n — and now the fiftieth term is one substitution away: two thousand six hundred. No listing. No guessing. One table, two difference rows, and every quadratic pattern in the exam confesses.
visual_style: Numbers march across the screen as a staircase with growing steps; a magnifying glass sweeps down to the second row of gaps where glowing 2s pulse in rhythm; the formula assembles piece by piece like evidence pinned to a detective's board.
pacing: Building tension through the growing jumps, sudden calm at the steady twos, brisk confident assembly of the formula.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and make every quadratic pattern confess its general term.
